answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create -n myAccount -g myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is part of the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }). Terraform (AzureRM): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" resource_group_name = "rg" location = "westus2" offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
Typical MongoDB-style connection string for Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB API):
mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&appName=@<account>@
You can also use SRV form if supported: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&replicaSet=globaldb. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true or tls=true) and replicaSet=globaldb and retrywrites is commonly set to false.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB API for MongoDB) primarily uses provisioned throughput charged in Request Units/sec (RUs) or autoscale RUs; serverless mode is also available for some APIs. Historically you can provision RU/s per database or per container; there are autoscale and serverless options. (There are also higher-capacity dedicated SKUs/tiers for large Mongo workloads in some offerings, but typical billing is RU-based.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API the common method is SCRAM (username/password) using the Cosmos account user credentials (the Mongo username and the account primary/secondary key as the password) supplied in the MongoDB connection string. The MongoDB API typically does not support native Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) DB authentication the way Azure SQL does; drivers authenticate with SCRAM credentials embedded in the connection string (or via connection options).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g. pymongo for Python). There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure client SDK for application data plane access — use the official MongoDB driver against the Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) Mongo endpoint. Use Azure SDKs only for management/ARM operations.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer:
Expect MongoDB-style k-NN/vector indexes (the createIndex syntax used by MongoDB 7+). Example (Mongo-like): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knn: { method: 'hnsw', space: 'cosinesimil', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } })
(Concrete options and supported methods vary by service build — common methods: HNSW, IVF, DiskANN — created via createIndex on the vector field with a knn/index options block.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search are typically done by integrating Azure Cognitive Search with the Cosmos DB dataset, or by using the MongoDB API's built-in text indexes for simple text search. For advanced hybrid ranking (text+vector) use Azure Cognitive Search (or an external search engine) that can index documents from Cosmos DB and combine vector search with text scoring.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Support depends on the chosen account 'server version' when the account is created; historically Cosmos DB exposed compatibility with specific MongoDB server versions (e.g. 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, later 5.x/6.x in some regions). Not all server features are supported: some admin commands, server-side JavaScript ($where), certain aggregation stages or extensive server-side file system integrations, and some background admin operations may be limited or unsupported. Expect a subset of MongoDB features; test critical features (transactions, change streams, specific aggregation stages) against the target account version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for the MongoDB API feature set. For development use a local MongoDB server (official mongo Docker image) on the standard port 27017, or test against a cloud test account. The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows/Docker) historically supports Core (SQL) API and not all MongoDB API features, so prefer a local mongo:5/6 container for driver-level tests on port 27017.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change Streams (MongoDB-style) are not reliably supported across all Cosmos DB Mongo API versions. Cosmos DB has its own Change Feed feature for the Core API which is supported and can be used instead. If you need MongoDB change streams, test against the specific account version; otherwise use Cosmos DB Change Feed for change notifications (no special enablement beyond creating containers).

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile for data-plane inspection and tools specific to the DocumentDB/Cosmos DB Mongo API cluster. The general Azure MCP server/profile handles ARM and management plane tasks, but a service-specific 'documentdb' MCP server gives data-plane helpers (collection/index inspection, query plans) as described in the run environment.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally named its NoSQL service 'DocumentDB'. That service was later subsumed and rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB API became Cosmos DB Core API). The term 'DocumentDB' historically refers to Microsoft's original proprietary service and is distinct from any similarly named open-source projects; the MongoDB API on Azure is an emulation layer over Cosmos DB (or a managed Mongo offering), not the open-source DocumentDB project.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath the MongoDB API the engine is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB implementation emulating the MongoDB wire protocol (i.e. a proprietary engine exposing Mongo endpoints). That means most MongoDB drivers work, but you may hit behavioral differences or unsupported commands; expect to use standard Mongo drivers but validate features/commands (transactions, change streams, aggregations) against the target account.

answers.question: Which database and collections will the sample use?
answers.answer: The sample will use the database named sample_retail_09 and create/use these collections: sales_velocity, suppliers, purchase_orders, and agent_memory.

answers.question: How will the application obtain and use the connection string at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the cluster connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it directly to the MongoDB driver (pymongo.MongoClient). Never hard-code the URI in files; provide .env.example with a placeholder.

answers.question: Which Python client will the sample use and what connection code will be used?
answers.answer:
Use the official pymongo library. Example code at startup: from pymongo import MongoClient
client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'])
db = client['sample_retail_09']

answers.question: What index definition does this sample expect for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a k-NN vector index on the embedding field of a products-like collection. Example Mongo-style createIndex: db.sales_velocity.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knn: { method: 'hnsw', space: 'cosinesimil', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — adjust options to the cluster-supported method (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN).

answers.question: How will the sample avoid duplicate purchase orders across agents?
answers.answer: Use a shared agent_memory collection (agent_memory) in sample_retail_09 to store keys of in-flight orders and finished orders. Orchestrator will check agent_memory for an existing purchase-order key before writing a new purchase_orders document; writes should use upsert with a unique deduplication key to avoid duplicates.
